text: Chapter 3 covered roles, least privilege, segregation of duties, and access reviews as separate topics. An access governance model is what you get when you stop treating them as five separate lessons and design them as one connected system.

Role definitions start from job function, not from copying someone else's access. Least-privilege mapping scopes each role to the minimum it actually needs. Segregation-of-duties rules define which role combinations are never allowed on one person. And a request and approval workflow, backed by periodic recertification, makes sure access is granted deliberately and reviewed on a schedule.

Here's a segregation-of-duties rule written down concretely: creating a vendor and approving vendor payments never combine on one person. That rule gets checked at request time, before access is granted — and recertification catches it if the combination ever appears later anyway.

Brightfield's incident traced to exactly two missing pieces from this model: no approval workflow requiring a named, scoped justification — access was granted on an informal ask — and no recertification cadence that would have caught the still-active login after the contract ended.
Next lesson, the course's closing lesson: privacy impact assessments — assessing the risk before you build something, instead of discovering it afterward.
